maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: The House resumed from Wednesday, February 11, consideration of the motion of Sir Eugene Fiset for an Address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his Speech at the opening of the session.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when six o'clock was called yesterday I had dwelt somewhat on the concentration of wealth and industry and the control of the different policies of this Dominion in certain areas. Still, in that connection I want to say a word on the question of Senate reform. The Speech from the Throne would indicate that very little can be done regarding that matter at this session of parliament. This may come as a disappointment to some of us who heard the speeches of the Prime Minister in western Canada. Of course it could hardly be expected that this House could, or would, pass a bill limiting the power of the Senate and expect the upper chamber to accept the same in toto. Furthermore, there are so many in public life to-day that look upon the Senate as a haven of rest from the uncertainties of party warfare as to make it possible that even here a measure to reform the Senate might have to follow a very tortuous course indeed. After all, an appeal to the provinces is the most constitutional way to proceed about the reforming of the Senate, and, perhaps, it also relieves the government from responsibility in the matter to some extent. Then the odium of changing the British North America Act would rest upon the provincial governments. But since the matter of Senate reform has not been discussed before the provincial electorate I cannot yet see how the existing provincial legislatures can, without at least a mandate from the people, deal competently with this question. The only benefit, therefore, that I can see to be derived from such a pronouncement is that the government will deal with Senate reform at some indefinite time in the future after there has been opportunity of asking the electorate to give them a mandate for carrying out the policy. As far as I am able to gather from a reading of a history of this country prior to confederation the one idea of the purpose of the Senate in the minds of the statesmen of the Maritimes, previous to those provinces entering confederation, was that a second chamber would prevent the exercise of any undue domination by the old provinces of Ontario and Quebec over the smaller provinces. I stated yesterday that the provinces of Ontario and Quebec have

The Address-Mr. Evans
dominated the rest of the Dominion ever since confederation. They have concentrated the wealth and the industry of the whole country within their own boundaries, and this domination they have so far maintained. Now looking over some of the speeches on Senate reform in years gone by, as reported in Hansard, I came across some utterances of that great Canadian statesman Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and the following is taken from a speech which he made in the House in 1906:
For my part I believe this abolition of the Senate-
Which was then under discussion.
-would be a mistake, and I could not be induced to reconcile myself to such an idea. A second chamber seems to me absolutely necessary for two reasons. It is supposed to be a check on hasty legislation. But one consideration, which to my mind, is absolutely conclusive and paramount is that, under our present system of government, composed of federal parts, a second chamber is an absolutely necessary safeguard against a possible invasion of their-
The smaller provinces.
-rights by the larger provinces. But if we are to have reform I would not be averse to adopting the system of our neighbours and having each province represented by an equal number of members whether that province be large or small.
Another reference was made in a speech made in the session of 1907-8. From that speech, as reported at page 1569 of Hansard, I take the following:
In the United States Senate, the state of New York has two members and the state of Rhode-Island has also two members, so that while in the House of Representatives each state speaks according to the numerical strength of its population, 36 against 2; in the Senate each state has an equal voice.
The only reform of the Senate that can ever prove acceptable to the provinces which go to make up the Dominion is to reconstruct that body, so that all the provinces shall be represented on the floor of the Senate by an equal number of representatives. There are nine provinces in this Dominion, and if each province was represented let us say, by five senators, that would give us a senate of 45 members. I think, Sir, that would be sufficiently large, without being too cumbersome. To curtail the power of the Senate, as at present constituted, by an alteration in the act stipulating that in the event of a bill passing this House twice it should become law even against the will of that body, would in my opinion be of very little benefit to this country, except in very isolated cases. Let me give an example. The fight is on in this country at present between public ownership and private ownership of public utilities. The Senate has twice during the life of this parliament thrown out bills for the construction of very much needed branch lines in
western Canada. This has been done in the interests of private ownership. Simply curtailing the power of the Senate as afore-mentioned would still give the privately owned concern an advantage of at least one year to choose their territory and to construct their lines practically on- the grade of the publicly owned company's survey. Two notable cases of this kind are seen in Saskatchewan to-day in the construction of the Lanigan and the Tuffnell branches.
Let me ask, is equality of representation in the Senate desirable? Domination of one province by another inevitably leads to sectionalism, and after fifty-seven years of a union which this country has experienced, a union that has not developed unity, confederation is heard cracking in different parts at the present time. There are ominous sounds even of separation to be heard. Ontario and Quebec, the old federation, have assumed an ownership of this Dominion that has at last become unbearable to the smaller provinces. For instance, to build a transcontinental railway they gave away to the first one of these railway companies 25,000,000 acres of land, belonging to Saskatchewan and Alberta, that never belonged to this Dominion. Every province was to come into confederation on an equal basis. The new Dominion of 1867 held in trust the Northwest Territories until such time as * the population there would warrant the forming of provinces. The older provinces assumed ownership, which they still hold so far as the natural resources are concerned. They even created hardship on the settlers in that part of the country by tax exemption of these lands, and the settlers themselves have had to meet this burden and pay the taxes themselves on that land to establish schools, construct roads and build bridges. Some 40,000,000 acres altogether of our lands have been alienated from their rightful owner to construct transcontinental railways in this Dominion. Now, placing the value of that land at $25 an acre, it would amount to the huge sum of $1,000,000,000 which will have to be taken into account when the question of natural resources comes up for settlement. Possession of power to dominate has made it difficult for these two provinces, Ontario and Quebec, to take an ocean-to-ocean view of Canada. They have habituated themselves into thinking of Canada in terms of two provinces only. Sectionalism can only be met and combated by sectionalism, which accounts for the feeling of disunity prevailing throughout the Dominion to-day.
The government can make a record for itself now by championing Senate reform on a constitutional basis so that real union will be established. In the absence of any con-
The Address-Mr. Evans

stitutional machinery to compel compromise, the inevitable result is the domination of the smaller by the larger provinces. A Senate of the type which Sir Wilfrid Laurier would have offered would be able to compel compromise and prevent domination. Can anyone conceive of what use excessive Senate representation is to Ontario and Quebec if not for the purpose of controlling, or having control of both the House of Commons and the Senate and the domination of other provinces? I say that no one need strain his imagination envisioning a truculent Prince Edward Island dominating Ontario and Quebec by means of its equal representation in the Senate; Rhode Island does not dominate New York, and New York cannot dominate Rhode Island.
I would also advocate that the new Senate be an elected body. Then the smaller provinces will be represented in that chamber, not by men chosen by Ontario and Quebec as at present, but by men of their own choice. The constitution of the country is the expression of the will of its own people. Elected representatives of the people have an inherent right and authority to speak for themselves; appointed members of legislative bodies have not. Even that historic body the House of Lords, whose forbears, the barons in arms, forced their king to sign the great charter, has been on occasions forced to bow to the will of the people. It is high time in this Dominion, in this democratic age, that we take steps to ensure a return of this power to the people of Canada and so amend the constitution that it will not be alienated.
TJntil such a reform is brought about, sectionalism will become more and more acute. While the domination of Ontario and Quebec in the past has been made perfectly secure by party domination in the provinces, this question bids fair now to cut even across party lines, and I dhall not be at all surprised to see solid provincial blocs occupying seats in this House until such a reform is brought about. I believe the reasonable thing to do is to call a conference at which each province will be represented by an equal number. Let us hope that such a conference will evolve an agreement that our constitution may be amended in such a way, and to the end, tlhat the people of Canada may be united for all time in a real federal union.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like other members who have preceded me, I offer my very sincere congratulations to the mover and the seconder of this Address. The hon. member for West Hastings (Mr. Hanna), fresh from his laurels in a hard-won battle, has added

further to his laurels by reason of his speech in this House. To the hon. member for Rim-ouski (Sir Eugene Fiset) perhaps I may be permitted to address a more personal note. He comes from that province Which has been my home and the home of my family for many generations, a province to which I and my family are attached root and branch in the same way as the French Canadians are there to this day, a province in which we Englishspeaking Canadians have learned to respect and to admire our French Canadian brothers. More than that, we have come to realize that this country is all the richer and greater by reason of having that great nation as one of our parts.
It may be properly said of talmost any country, and particularly of a new country like Canada, that a country's wealth and progress are measured by the extent of and increase in its population. As a matter of fact, that saying is not very difficult to analyze, when one realizes that production can take place only by means of population, and it follows from that, that the greater the population, the greater will be the production and, consequently, the greater the production, the greater the wealth of the country.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Does that apply to China?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes, that applies to Chinamen too, if my hon. friend wants an answer immediately. Production, however, to take place at all, certainly to be continuous, must be profitable. It must be profitable, at least to the extent that the producer is able to gain a livelihood by means of his production. From that it follows that if production is profitable, more will seek an occupation in which such profit exists. On the other hand, where that profit is not apparent or where that profit does not exist, there will be a diminution and finally an entire cessation in production and population as a consequence will decline. It may be very properly assumed from that that profitable production will increase population, and increased population will increase production, and increased production will produce greater wealth. But we must bear in mind that profitable production is very distinctly limited by certain factors, one of them being the effect of taxation. If taxation, no matter how applied, is taken off the profit on an article, then the profit is less. If it is added to the cost of an article, that cost may amount to so much as to make the article itself unprofitable. Another factor which limits production is the possibility of marketing the thing produced, that is to say,


The Address-Mr. Marler
turning it into money or exchanging it for another suitable article which the producer might require. I freely admit that these principles are extremely elementary, in fact so elementary that I hesitate to assert them in this House; but notwithstanding that, I think hon. members will agree with me that on the successful and proper application of these principles really depends the success of any nation.
You have only to apply these principles, for example, to our natural resources, which are the real basic wealth of this country. Without those natural resources neither this nor any other country can prosper. But of what use are our natural resources unless they are developed, unless they are applied to useful purposes? While they remain in the ground they are of no value whatever. Even when those natural resources are made into products, those products still cannot be established as regards their value unless there is the ability to market them to people who desire to acquire them. The same thing applies to any industry, no matter whether that industry be foodstuffs, labour, manufactured goods, or anything else.
As I started out to say a moment ago production is limited by certain factors, one of them being taxation. We have heard it stated throughout the country that our taxation has been limiting production; that it has been driving capital from the country; more than that, that it has been preventing people from coming here, and that it has had various other results too numerous to mention. As a matter of fact, some of those results deserve a great deal of consideration; but while to reduce taxation is an extremely easy thing to say, it is a very difficult thing to accomplish. Those who say that and who say reduce taxation at all costs, cannot be as well acquainted with the finances of this country, the needs of its finances and the needs of the distribution of its revenue as they should be. It is not to be wondered at that the people of this country do not know more about the necessity of our taxes and of the distribution of the revenues. When we realize that before the war we had only two sources of taxation, namely, customs and excise, we can come to the conclusion that the ordinary man in the street knew little or nothing about taxes. He had, perhaps, a hazy idea that certain taxes were imposed and that some taxes were necessary to run the country, but where they came from he had no idea. As we proceeded and even as we went on with the war the general public did not realize that new taxes were being imposed. They were at that time interested in many other affairs- great expenditures of money were going abroad, and even at that time they did not realize that taxation existed in the form in which it does to-day. But after the war, when we had arrived at more normal times, the public realized to the full and in the most potent way imaginable that there were taxes and heavy taxes at that.
They realized that nothing could be done and that no business could be prosecuted without first of all solving the problem of taxation. And at last it came to be borne in upon the public, a thing which should have been realized and appreciated long before by poor and rich alike, that a tax, no matter how imposed or how collected, is finally borne by the consumer in some form or another. In other words, the man buying from the corner grocery store or from the nearby butcher pays the tax directly or indirectly on what he purchases in exactly the same way as he pays it who buys from the rich city merchant or from the high class jeweller: everyone bears the tax or taxes in proportion to the amount consumed by him in his supplies for his daily needs. There is no getting away from this; in the last analysis, that is where the tax must be borne, no matter-how it may be imposed. That being the case, the public became vitally interested in our questions of taxation as well as in our problems of revenue, and they became interested also in the question as to how our expenditures were made. Concerning these matters of interest the public were in a state of confusion. Indeed, the public at the present moment do not sufficiently realize and certainly do not sufficiently appreciate our necessity for revenue nor the need of our expenditures, and I do not think that this confusion and this lack of knowledge can be particularly wondered at; because, after all, although our public accounts are published in a perfectly fair and intelligible manner, easily accessible to members of parliament, and quite open and correct to the expert accountant who cares to look into them, and although they are kept most carefully and faithfully by efficient officials of the department, they are nevertheless published nowadays in such a way that the ordinary man in the street is unable at a glance to understand them. The average taxpayer has neither the time nor the ability, nor has he the opportunity to delve into these accounts as fully as he should in order to get some grasp of public affairs and to realize what revenue is necessary and what expenditure indispensable. It seems to me that we should publish at the end of every fiscal year a simple statement of our accounts so that
The Address-Mr. Marler

the public may obtain the facts and fully realize and appreciate exactly what our taxes are needed for, and how our revenue has been spent. This is done in connection with the British exchequer, which publishes a small leaflet explaining the various revenues from taxes, excise, sendees, and so forth, showing, not in too great detail but sufficiently to enable the average taxpayer to understand a month or so after the end of the fiscal year, precisely how the taxes are paid and exactly how the expenditures have been made. Unless we take the public into our confidence to that extent and advise them fully as regards our receipts and disbursements, I fail to understand how we can expect them to have an intelligent grasp of the affaire of the country.
I want to pass now to the Speech from the Throne, and before I do so I shall introduce a personal note into the remarks I am about to make. I do not think that any hon. member on the other side of the House can charge me with any lack of candour, nor do I think that any hon. gentleman on this side can accuse me of speaking at any time except in tones of sincerity, although, perhaps in tones of too great independence. But if that independence has been invoked, let me say that it has been asserted simply because of my belief in Liberalism. Liberals all the world over have been free; they have not been bound by any hard and fast or immutable rules, but rather have always been allowed to exercise their judgment as their consciences might dictate. And I can say that I speak with such candour when I declare that having examined the Speech from the Throne I am able to express the opinion that it shows very great vision, far greater vision indeed than has characterized many speeches which I have seen published in many a long day.

speechtext:
I will take up with the exMinister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) various figures with a view to finding out what is controllable and what is uncontrollable, and also what this government is liable for as against what can be charged to the responsibility of the hon. gentleman's government. I should like, if I may have the permission of the House, to place on Hansard in full a statement, which I shall read briefly, so that hon. gentlemen may have the facts before them. This is a very simple statement, but I have prepared it with the object in view of taking it up item by item and discussing exactly what our expenses have been, so that we may decide for ourselves the accuracy or otherwise of what is therein set forth. Receipts for the fiscal year ending 31 March, 1924, were as follows:
Receipts for the fiscal year ending 31 March, 1924:
A.	From ordinary sources not
war-consisting entirely of customs and excise-and a comparatively small sum from interest on investments-and excluding revenue from services in departments..	.. 165,3-15,546
B.	From war taxes-such as income, business, profits, sales, cheques, receipts, transportation, trust and loan companies, banks and interest on advances to Imperial and
foreign governments	 204,862,739



The Address-Mr. Marler
are taken from the public accounts. The controllable expenditure of 1914 amounted to $78,397,000, and in 1924 it was $103,000,000; an increase of $25,000,000.
Now, Sir, I do not say that our expenditure in 1924 was as low as it should have been.
I believe at that time that we had got into very extravagant ways. But that is not the point at all. The point is that the public became used to certain services in 1914, the war intervened, the value of the d'ollar depreciated very much indeed, and the real comparison of the public wants to-day is between the cost of the services they had before the war and the cost of the same services to-day. The figure which I have given of $25,000,000 is the increased cost of those services.
But I want to go a step further, with all due regard to my friends opposite. In that controllable expenditure are certain items for which this government was in no way responsible, and I am treating the fact with the utmost candour and the utmost sincerity, because I believe t)he public should foe put in possession of the facts irrespective of everything else. In that $25,000,000 there were items such as expenditure on our merchant marine, the Canada Highways Act and the Victoria shipowners, amounting to over $6,000,000, which leaves the difference between the controllable expenditure in 1914 and in 1924, for which this government is responsible, at the sum of $19,000,000. Now, if you realize the reduced value of the dollar, if you compute quickly in your mind the fact that the controllable expenditure for the selfsame service was $78,000,000 in 1914, you cannot say that an increase of $19,000,000 is out of all proportion for the year 1924.
Much has been said and much has been written on the question of departmental expenditure, the cost of the departments has been criticized to a very great extent in the public press and elsewhere, and it has been said that we have retained in the departments many officials whose services might well be dispensed with, that the cost has been built up to an extraordinary extent, and as a consequence the country was being deprived of revenue and paying taxation which should not have been imposed upon it. Well, the net cost of the departments-because it is only right to take off revenue derived from the services of some of them-in 1914 was $65,000,000, While in 1924 it was $86,000,000, or an increase of approximately $20,000,000, which does not seem to be excessive. I do not say that an attempt should not be made to bring the cost down, but owing to the vast increase in what has to be collected, when we 
realize that the revenue from taxes in 1914 amounted to $128,000,000, as against $370,000,000 in 1924, when we realize that the disbursements in 1914 were $185,000,000, and in 1924 $334,000,000, we cannot say that the cost of government to-day is a great deal more than it should be or that the cost can be severely cut down.
There is another question that I desire to take up before leaving these figures, a question that I have looked into with some care, and one in which I think not only hon. members but the public generally have some concern. Indeed, my right hon. friend who leads the opposition (Mr. Meighen) brought this matter up in his address a few days ago. He was quoting, as he will remember, Speeches from the Throne of other years. He quoted from the Speech of 1923, and he used these terms:
Do you realize, Mr. Speaker, why none of these are mentioned this year ?
He was speaking about revenue and expenditure.
For the simple reason that the condition in every instance is distinctly the opposite: instead of a decline in the public expenditure and an increase in the public revenue there has been to date a decline of $50,000,000 odd in the public revenue and an increase of $2,300,000 in public expenditure.
Surely my right hon. friend is not going to take the figures with respect to the middle of the year and come to the conclusion that they are a criterion of what the expenditure will be for the whole year. Moreover, why should he glory in the suggestion that there has been a reduction in revenue? The only reason there has been a reduction in revenue, is simply because this government- has made an attempt, and an honest attempt, to reduce taxes. But further than that, if he will examine the figures with respect to the last year that his government was in power he will find that there was a reduction of $54000,000 in the revenue in that year. So I do not think his criticism in that regard is well founded. In order to make a fair comparison I submit that it would be proper to take two years of the administration of this government and two year3 of the administration. of the previous government, that is to say, the fiscal years ending March 31, 1921 and March 31, 1922, which were under the control of the previous government, and the fiscal years ending March 31, 1923 and March 31, 1924, which were under the control of this government. A comparison of those figures, would, it seems to me, be eminently fair in every way. I have made that comparison, and I would like also to have this table put upon Hansard:

Now, I want to return to the question that I started out first of all to speak about, and to which the Speech from the Throne also makes reference in very clear and distinct language. I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, that these figures are so terribly unpalatable, but they have to be given in order to make this point quite clear. The Speech from the Throne says:
It is apparent that even the most rigid economy in public expenditures will not suffice to solve this pressing problem and the problem of taxation incidental thereto.
_ That is another general statement, and it is correct. An examination of the public accounts for the year, item by item, will show that it is practically impossible to cut off expenditure under any of those items. Take our war taxes, which in 1924 amounted to $370,000,000: these taxes were in payment of our war debt and in payment also of our pensions and of administration as regards war services. It is true we had a surplus in that respect of $50,000,000. While on the question of war taxes may I suggest to the government that if at all possible these taxes in respect to war services be segregated from all others. The people have borne these taxes, have endured their stagnating influence for many years without a murmur, and they 4 p.m. have done that because they have felt that these were war taxes and 8i
for war purposes. I do not say it is possible to do it, but if it could be done it would be highly desirable to segregate them for that particular purpose. The war debt could then be gradually eliminated1 and the taxes correspondingly reduced.
Taking our ordinary taxes, of which I have spoken previously, these represented expenditures connected with the cost of the departments, the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, highways, and other items-for the present I leave out railway expenditure. The large increase in that class of taxation is without a doubt represented by the interest on the non-war debt. In 1914 the interest on the non-war debt amounted in round figures to $13,000,000; in 1924 it amounted to $29,000,000, an increase of $16,000,000.
I do not want to go back particularly to the past for the purpose of dealing with our past expenditures, but we are all well aware of what happened at the beginning of this century. We were all imbued with the idea that the twentieth century was to be "Canada's century." You heard that from the Atlantic to the Pacific; everybody had it, rich and poor, young and old. As a consequence we involved ourselves in vast expenditures. We increased our manufacturing plants. We trebled our railways. We urged our farmers in the west to hurry up, to take up more land, to extend their activities, and this of course, involved the requirement of greater credits. But the public have been inclined to say: "Oh, it is the politicians who have done all this. It is the politicians who have been responsible for all this expenditure, the politicians who have asked us to enter upon this extravagance." Well, Sir, all I can say in that regard is this:	Remember what happened in connection with the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific and the National Transcontinental. Examine, ' if you will, the resolutions of boards of trade in all parts of this country, which begged and prayed the government of that day to proceed with the construction of the National Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific. Examine what railway men like Wainwright and Hays said. Examine the petition to the government signed by Wainwright, Hays and the late Senator Cox, who said that with all possible speed the new railway should be built from the Atlantic to the Pacific. More than that, you can examine the various proceedings of the Grand Trunk shareholders in England who, without a dissenting voice and with prolonged cheers, declared that the Grand Trunk Pacific project was not only necessary for Canada but necessary for the saving of the Grand Trunk itself. These were their words at the shareholders'
The Address-Mr. Marler

meetings. That being the ease, it seems foolish for the public not to realize that they have been just as much responsible as the government of that day and the governments that followed for the expenditures which did take place in this connection.
In discussing this particular paragraph in the Speech from the Throne, and the truth in substance of that statement, we must remember that this vast expenditure in the days gone by has had a very pronounced effect upon the taxation of the present. Our expenditure in those days was out of all reason; it was a mad, drunken orgy of expenditure, and we are paying for it now in taxation which we cannot escape. We entered upon all these enterprises with our eyes wide open and there is no reason why we should now go into mourning and say we did not realize what was going on.
Take, for example, the figures as regards capital expenditure, and I may say the comparisons I am about to give are of very considerable interest. In the five yearn from 1896 to 1900 we expended in railway subsidies and in building canals, harbours and docks some $34,000,000. In the period from 1901 to 1905 we increased that capital expenditure to $54,000,000. In the five years from 1906 to 1910 that expenditure increased from $54,000,000 to $134,000,000. From 1911 to 1915, entirely exclusive of war outlays, our capital expenditure increased to $197,000,000; and from 1916 to 1920 it rose to $251,000,000.
As I say we cannot get away from paying the interest on these various obligations which we have incurred. I do not think we can very seriously cut down departmental expenditure, as one can see from a careful analysis of that expenditure. There have been increases in the expenditure of the great departments, for example, of Customs and Excise, Post Office and Finance. There have been great increases in the revenue collected, and great increases in the services. In other departments, such as Agriculture, Interior, and Health, again there have been increases, but those increases, Mr. Speaker, are due, in so far as anyone can see to the demands from the public for the rendering of certain services, and expenditure cannot be cut down in these departments unless the public itself is willing to do without the services which it had before the year 1914. We can make up our minds to that situation very clearly and very distinctly. If we want those services we have to pay for them. That expenditure must be met by taxation, and that taxation must come out of the pockets of the people. tMr. Marler.]
There is one item which I hesitate I admit to speak about in this House but which it seems to me should be spoken about no matter how unpopular it may be. A very good plan, very earnest gesture on our part would be to cut down our own indemnities.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I do not hear any great
applause to that suggestion.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: We will help you.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
May I put a question
to the hon. gentleman whose speech I am enjoying very much?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: He mentions this plan of retrenchment. I would ask is not the increase in uncontrollable expenditure largely due to the increase of salaries?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It has been increased to
some extent by salaries, to the cost of living bonus and the betterment of salaries, but the public services have grown to a very large extent. These services were asked for by the public and the public is now paying for them. However, I am quite serious in this respect: A very effective measure would be to cut down our own indemnities. If we want to cut down taxes why should we not give that gesture to the public and say we are willing to cut down our indemnity. Why should we go to our constituencies and say "You cannot have this and cannot have that," and yet keep for ourselves the increase that was made in our indemnities. There is no reason why we should not do as I suggest, no reason why we should not give an example to the rest of the country by doing it.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: By what amount would you suggest the indemnity should be reduced?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
According to the number
of children.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
In answer to my hon.
friend from Southeast Grey I would reduce the indemnity to the amount it was before the war.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in brief let me repeat what I said a few moments ago as to reducing taxation by cutting down expenditure: While we may be able to cut down that expenditure in part, while we may be able to cut down capital expenditure in part, while we may be able to do without some of these services

The Address-Mr. Marler
which I think we should do without, while we may be able to cut down our own indemnities-all that is a drop in the bucket as regards the reduction in taxation. And again the Speech from the Throne is correct when it says:
It is apparent that even the most rigid economy in public expenditures will not suffice to solve this pressing problem and the problem of taxation incidental thereto.
So we come down to the point, also stated in t)he Speech from the Throne that this expenditure and this taxation the country is undergoing to-day is due to one main cause and that cause is the encumbered position of our National Railways. Had we not our railway expenditure, had we not to put forward every year large sums of money on our railways, had we not to build those railways up as they have had to be built up under both governments-I am not complaining about what the other government did-and had we not to put aside 'this huge sum of money every year-I want to make this point clear and distinct to every member of the House-we would have a surplus that we could apply as regards reduction in taxation. We could see our way clear to a reduction of taxation and in time a very considerable reduction in taxation if the railway problem was not on our hands.
That being the case let us discuss for a moment the Canadian National Railways, and then I will pass on to another subject. The Canadian National Railways, as every member knows, is an amalgamation of four separate groups-the old Canadian Government railways, the Canadian Northern, the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk. These railways during their separate existence incurred very many obligations. These obligations were incurred by the railways, they were not directly assumed by us, but other obligations were directly guaranteed. Other obligations were contracted from time to time in the names of the railways guaranteed by the Dominion, or contracted by the Dominion itself for railway purposes. The point I want to make is this: It does not seem to make any difference whether we actually assumed these particular debts which the railways had at the time, whether these particular debts were incurred by the Canadian National Railway in its present corporate capacity or indirectly by the government. All these debts of the railways have, as a matter of fact, become the obligation of this country. I am not discussing the question of accounts at all, I am simply discussing a practical business matter. Here we have these railways. We own them. When we took them over, as I
have said, they had a considerable funded debt secured on the lines and ranking prior to many of the obligations which we ourselves had guaranteed. Those securities, issued against the various parts of the line-and I will again ask permission to put the schedule explaining them into Hansard-amount to $328,000,000. After that there were securities guaranteed by ourselves to the extent of $470,000,000. That is to say the total securities which we would have .to pay before we could recoup ourselves for any cash we put into these lines amount to $798,000,000. In addition to that we advanced to these Various bodies, either separately or to the system as a whole, another $773,000,000 and we expended on the Canadian government group $494,000,000. To strike a balance, although I do not think it is correctly insertable, Canadian Northern 5 per cent income stock, which only bears interest in the event of its earning, to the amount of $24,000,000 appears in the schedule referred to. But leaving that amount in there is involved in these railways the huge sum of $2,000,000,000.

The Address-Mr. Marler

I want to impress upon hon. members of this House just exactly what that railway situation is, and also that in order to work out a reduction an taxation, the railway situation must be solved at all hazards. That is the crux of the whole situation. I do not think the railways are making the progress they should make under present conditions, and that progress is not being made, not because the management is not doing its utmost, not because the government is not doing its utmost to help that management, but simply because it is impossible for the railways under present conditions to increase their traffic earnings. It is quite true that an improvement has been made. In 1920 there was a deficit of fixed charges of $26,000,000 and at the end of 1923 that had been turned into a surplus of $13,000,000. That would look in the first instance as though there had been an improvement of $39,000,000; but that was the operating improvement, and a very acceptable operating improvement it was, but you have to take off that operating improvement the fixed charges, to say nothing of the money which is owed to us. Take the fixed charges off and also take into consideration that during those four or .five years which I have had under review we expended, in order to make that increase, something like $314,000,000, losing the interest on that amount. There is $100,000,000 in interest still unpaid, and the net gain in the years in question, you will find after working it out in the most careful way, has not been greater than $16,-
500,000.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Does the hon.
gentleman not think that a rearrangement of the service between the two great systems might not materially cut down the cost of operation?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes, without a doubt. I will come to that in a moment. I daresay that this large expenditure which is being incurred by the railways every year may not have to go on. Perhaps we have got to a point when the trains will stay on the tracks now; but in any event that expenditure may have to be continued. But let me say, Mr. Speaker, that the people of this country have got to the limit of their endurance with regard to taxation, and they wiil not, I can assure you, Sir, stand for very much more expenditure for spectacular locomotives, or spectacular advertising or radios or matters of that description. All these pleasing little things will have to be cut out, because the people of this country have reached the limit of their endurance.

I will now take up the question asked me by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth)-railway competition. I had made a note in regard to that question. As we all know in this country we have the two great railway systems, the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National. Now we want healthy and fair competition between these two railways, and it is in our interest to have such a healthy and fair competition but it is not in our interest to have stupid competition, it is not in our interest to have duplication, nor is it in our interest to have a spectacular movement on the part of any of these great railway companies. It is not in our interest to have so many trains run on one line and an equal number of trains run on the other line in the same territory. There is no sense in it and no object to be gained in so far as the Canadian National Railway is to be concerned. Nor is there any object to be gained so far as the Canadian Pacific is concerned. Unless these two railways come to some agreement themselves, it seems to me it is high time that parliament should step in and make them come to some sensible agreement, in order that the foolish duplication should not be continued.
Now let us ask ourselves how this railway problem can be solved. I again turn to the Speech from the Throne which says:
Their ultimate solution lies largely in increased production and the development of new and wider markets.
There is no question about that at all. It is the only way we can solve our railway problem. We can do what we will, we can spend as much money as we will, and we can avoid as much duplication as we will, but we will never solve the railway problem until we build up the country by more production and more profitable production. That is the only way we can solve our railway problem. Then we come back, Mr. Speaker, to the same old question and we face the vicious circle-exactly the same question. It is a question of more people, more hard work, more wise economy and less expenditure, which does not mean no expenditure at all. That is the position in which we find ourselves. That is the position in which we are after we analyze the situation in every possible way. After we go through every channel possible in regard to our expenditure in taxation, we come down again as I say to the question of more people, more profitable production and more hard work. I say that the people of this country are to-day looking to us to find out in what way we can relieve them of their problem. We stand challenged to-day by the people of this country to find in what

The Address-Mr. Marler
manner we can relieve them of the many pressing burdens, which burdens are not overwhelming, although they are serious and have to be taken into consideration. But the problem of procuring more people, the problem of keeping our young manhood in Canada and the problem of more profitable production, all of which are associated, and all of which are inter-dependent, might perhaps seem to some to be almost impossible to overcome. Those who hold that view, who say that these matters are overwhelming, and that they are insuperable, simply lack courage in their country; they do not realize that we have a sound, and a safe foundation on which to build. They do not realize that we have our natural resources and our other industries which by perseverance we have built up. They do not realize that we in this country are in a position to give diversified employment to everybody who may come here. The solution is to apply to those natural resources and to those industries policies which will conserve one and develop the other, and increase thereby profitable production, thereby attracting more people.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
That is not in
the Speech from the Throne.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The Speech from the
Throne makes precisely that statement in words which I will give the House.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman did not
read that paragraph.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
After the witticisms of
my hon. friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton) I will continue. These questions of profitable production and of securing more people for this country I admit are not without their difficulties, but the only way in which we can overcome them is by realizing those difficulties and doing our best to overcome them. We will never overcome them so long as we think in terms of Ontario and Quebec, or in terms of the east and the west. We have to think of them in terms of Canada and Canada only. That is the only way by which we will be able to overcome our difficulties in this country. These difficulties are known to you; perhaps they need not be repeated, but in order to continue the trend of my argument I am going to take the liberty of repeating some of them to the House, because they follow out very largely what I have been saying.
The first of these difficulties is our geographical situation. Canada is not a compact country. It is not a country with a moderately dense population; it is a country stretching across the continent with an extremely
scattered population, settled, perhaps, in a way in which it should never have been settled, but nevertheless, settled as it has been. In the United States, settlement was made gradually towards the west. In this country our settlement was far flung to all comers. This country, instead of being a compact country, one which could be easily governed, is, as a matter of fact, divided into four distinct parts, each of which is separated from the other by natural obstacles more or less difficult. We have the Maritimes separated from the industrial central provinces of Ontario and Quebec by a long stretch of sparsely settled country; we have the central provinces of Quebec and Ontario separated from the prairie section by a long stretch of wilderness, and we have the Pacific province of British Columbia, separated from the prairie section by the Rocky mountains. The division of this country in that particular way is not the only difficulty. In each of those particular divisions there has grown up different viewpoints, different industries, very often different from those in other parts of the country, and different economic views of life. Another difficulty is that we have along our *whole southern border the richest, one of the most populous nations of the world, constantly influencing us in many ways we do not perceive and do not understand, constantly acting as a magnet for our population, rendering our position in this country perhaps the most difficult of any country in the world.
All those influences give rise to various factors. Our widely scattered population and great distances give rise to questions of transportation; our different industries in the different parts of Canada give rise to questions of tariffs and our proximity to the United States gives rise to questions of labour, taxation and competition. With those various differences in the geographical situation and in the industrial life of this country, I cannot see how anybody can say that a fixed and decided policy can be formulated which will apply to the whole of Canada. A policy for example fashioned in the terms of the Maritimes might not suit the provinces of Ontario and Quebec; a policy fashioned in the terms of Ontario and Quebec might not suit the prairie section, and it is conceivable that a policy fashioned in the terms of the prairie sections might not suit other parts of Canada. What, therefore, should we attempt to do? We should fashion policies which would encourage as much as possible the basic industries in every part of the Dominion. But in doing that, someone will say to us: Yes, you encourage an industry there and you
The Address-Mr. Marler

discourage an industry elsewhere. In other words there is a conflict of interest, a conflict of economic forces. That may happen, it cannot be denied, with our far-flung population in the various parts of this country. But where a certain policy framed to encourage an industry in one particular section of the country prejudicially affects an industry in another section, the industry unfavourably affected should* be given some compensating factor in order that it may get on in the best way possible without feeling the burden unduly.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Would the speaker encourage some sort of zoning policy by which each section would be allowed to choose its own particular policy, protection or free trade?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Throne may perhaps be correctly used; but I do not think it is a term that can be properly applied as regards freight rates, because if equalization means a certain rate per mile, that cannot work out inasmuch as the topography of the country, the density of population and a hundred other questions must be considered. What we should bear in mind in the matter of freight rates is, as I say, not the question whether those rates compare with the rates in the United States or in any other country: we need rates that will enable the people to build up the basic industries and promote profitable production so that more people will be induced to enter the country without the necessity for an immigration policy at all.
Incidentally, while we are discussing this question of freight rates, two other questions will occur to us in that regard. The first question is, who is to make these rates; the second it, who is to bear the cost. Opinions may differ on the first question. Some will say that parliament should make the rates. If so, I find it extremely difficult to agree with that opinion. I venture to say that with the sole exception of my hon. friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton) none of us in this House has a general understanding of the complicated structure of freight rates. My hon. friend from Brandon (Mr. Forke) may know all about freight rates on farm products, my hon. friend from North Bruce (Mr. Malcolm) may know all about freight rates on furniture, some other of my hon. friends may know all about freight rates on other commodities, but who in this House is capable of taking into consideration comparisons between a ton mile, a freight mile and a passenger mile, what any particular traffic will bear, and half a hundred other questions that arise in this complex matter. We are incapable in this House or in a committee of making up a general structure of freight rates. But there is a body competent to make such a structure-the Board of Railway Commissioners. That body has made a study of freight rates and is competent to deal with the question. Let my point not be misunderstood in that regard, Mr. Speaker. I say the railway commission is the proper body to formulate the general basis of a rate structure; but no one will assert that we in this House should not say, for the purpose of assisting any basic industry in any part of the country, that a specific rate is not advisable in order to bring the product of that particular industry to market.
As to the second question, who is to bear the cost of lower freight rates that we might

decide on, this is an important factor also, and hon. gentlemen would be very well advised to take it into their most earnest consideration. Let them bear in mind that we have two great railway systems, the National and the Canadian Pacific, each attempting to the fullest extent of its ability to give good' service, but each struggling to live on account of insufficient traffic. To say to the National, reduce freight rates below the cost of living rates fixed by the railway commission, will simply mean that the deficits on that line will be greater, and its officers and employees will be faced with still greater discouragement. If a similar reduction is made in respect of freight rates of the Canadian Pacific, that line also will probably have a deficit, which will affect not only our national financial standing, but our financial standing internationally.
Anyone studying the subject will admit that on account of our geographic situation we must have such transportation rates as will enable the products of the various sections of this country to compete in the markets of the world. It is that geographical situation which we have to overcome, and I believe that any reduction below the general structure of freight rates as made by the railway commission should be borne by the country as a whole, for this reason. It is in the interests of the country generally to promote profitable production in the west and in the Maritimes, because the rest of the Dominion will benefit at the same time.
Now, I have spoken of compensating factors which may require to be given to various sections of the country. I have also spoken of the utter impossibility of formulating a blanket policy which will suit the whole Dominion. I admit freely that there are conflicting interests, and that these will continue until they are wiped out by more population. I do not intend to avoid discussing what perhaps is an unpleasant topic to some, therefore I do not intend to conceal my ideas on certain subjects. I have spoken to some extent and made an attempt to outline a policy as regards the prairie provinces and the Maritimes, but I have made no observations with respect to the central provinces of Quebec and Ontario. I am not anxious to refer to these sections, but I am confident that if I do not deal with them I shall be told I should have given my views with regard to them.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Before my hon. friend leaves the question of freight rates, I understood him to say that perhaps the chief factor in our heavy taxation is the deficits of the

The Address-Mr. Marler
National railway. Reduced freight rates east and west, as suggested by him, would necessarily increase those deficits, and I should like to ask him whether this would not aggravate the situation which he has already described as almost unbearable.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The point is well taken.
I attempted in the earlier part of my remarks to emphasize that we had locked up in the Canadian National lines a vast sum of money, that the system was not making the progress that it should make by the means at our command, and that the only way in which progress could be made was by having more production and therefore greater freight traffic. I also attempted to make the point that to have greater production we had to have more profitable production in order to attract people to settle in various parts of the Dominion. My claim is that it does not matter how much money we spend in immigration, it does not matter how much advertising we do to attract immigrants, unless people in every section of the country are prosperous it is not a bit of good to bi'ing more people into those sections. I admit that reduced freight rates will cost the country money, I admit that deficits in the meantime will likely increase, but I claim that when we have an increased population making profitable production those deficits will gradually' decrease until they are ultimately wiped out entirely.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Taxation in the meantime
may increase?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It may increase.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
You are not looping the
loop?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
If we do not loop the
loop some way we will loop ourselves another way pretty quickly.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I have followed the hon.
gentleman's remarks fairly well, but if freight rates to and from the Maritime provinces and the prairie provinces are lowered, it simply means that our taxation is going to be increased. The hon. gentleman stated that the consumer ultimately pays taxation. If this increased burden is cast upon the people of the two provinces of Ontario and Quebec, it means increased protection, and higher prices, and you are simply in a vicious circle; you cannot get out of it.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Of course it will cost more to lower railway rates. I said quite distinctly that the cost would be borne by the country as a whole, not necessarily-

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: By the consumer.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
By the consumer, yesby the country as a whole not by one particular section or another particular section. Let my hon. friend not misunderstand me:
I do not claim for a moment that this is an economic principle that can be defended; I do not think it can be defended in any way. But let me be quite frank in that respect: what is the alternative? What is to be done? How are we in this country to make production profitable? How are we to increase our population, first of all, so that these deficits may decrease? I do not claim that a suggestion of this description is a proper economic suggestion that one would make under any other circumstances.
We are well aware that a great part of the industry of the central provinces of Quebec and Ontario is bound up in manufacturing. All the urban population and many of those who comprise the rural population have interests which are bound up with the manufacturing industries. I want to put the claims of the people of these provinces, as I hear them and as I understand them, frankly and freely before hon. members of this House. I am not going to discuss the merits or demerits of fiscal systems; I am only going to put forward what may be regarded as a reasonable claim. These people say that in order to enable them to develop their various industries, a certain tariff should be maintained so that goods manufactured under more favourable climatic and other conditions than those applicable to goods manufactured in Canada shall not be dumped in here to undersell our Canadian made products. Now, I do not intend to debate the merits or demerits of the tariff systems which have been in vogue in this country. I know that those in certain sections of the country claim that the tariff system is no good, while on the other hand those in other sections say that its maintenance is imperative. But it seems to me that those living in the different parts of the country should know what is best for them; they are the best judges. The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) distinctly says, "No, this system will not do; we will have none of it." He went on to say, "When the population goes out into the west, see what is ahead of you." Now, I do not take these remarks of the hon. member for Brandon seriously. I think he is 5. p.m. too good a Scotchman and has too much sense not to view these matters in a fair light.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Let me correct my hon.
friend's statement. I said that when the
The Address-Mr. Marler

population was in the majority in the west they would probably treat the people in the east as the east now treat the people in the west.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Let us be frank about this thing. We want to try to get at some reasonable and common policy. What is the use of our bandying words across the floor of this House? What is the use of talking about this eastern and this western idea? Let us try to arrive at some common basis on which we can proceed. That is why I am talking here to-day and for no other reason. I would not be bothered talking on this subject at all if I were not desirous of making a reasonable attempt to offer you from the city of Montreal a fair, honest and decent gesture.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Does the hon. member ever find me talking in any other strain?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I was going on to say
that I did not for a moment take seriously what my hon. friend said in that respect. I do not for a moment take seriously what the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) is reported to have said. I do not think that hon. gentlemen in that quarter of the House have any less sense or any less intelligence than we have in the east; perhaps in some cases they have more. I believe they are just as good Canadians as we are in the east and that they have just as good ideas. I want to see the whole country go ahead. I believe our present differences are due to lack of understanding, to lack of clarity; to the fact that the conditions have not been put before the people of the west as clearly and as fairly as they should have been. That is why I am speaking this afternoon, as representing a part of the city of Montreal, directly to hon. members from the west.
We may as well recognize that there is that conflict of interests. But if it can be plainly shown that a reasonable d'evelopment tariff is necessary in the country, would it not be fair, if a transportation structure is borne by the remainder of the country, for certain parts to have in the meantime, until our population is built up, until our markets are increased, a reasonable tariff to develop these particular industries?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Would my hon. friend explain to the House how the manufacturers of Quebec and Ontario can get any benefit out of the tariff if they are going to compensate the west for the burden which that tarjff imposes on the west?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am not going to discuss theories with my hon. friend at all. I am
CMr. Forke.]
sick of theories on this thing I want to get down to plain business facts.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I think the question is a fair one.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Well, I d!o not understand it.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: May I repeat my question?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: My hon. friend may repeat it as much as he likes.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Would my hon. friend from Montreal explain how Ontario and Quebec, if they are advantaged at the present time through the tariff, are going to derive any permanent benefit from the tariff if they must pay compensation to the west?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes, I will explain that, certainly. Ontario and Quebec want to see the west populated and prosperous; that is why.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Wipe out the tariff, then.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Wipe out the tariff? My hon. friend is again getting into theories. We have had enough theories from my hon. friend during the last three years in this House; we do not know where we are as regards his theories.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I notice that.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Let us get down to facts.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Build the Hudson Bay railway.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes, if the Hudson Bay railway is shown to be a good thing I shall be the first to favour it. Certainly I will, but I want to be shown by proper proof that the Hudson Bay railway would be all that it should be. I will support the Hudson Bay railway or anything else for the good of the west if it is shown to be right, but I am not going to support the theories which some of my hon. friends opposite advance.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: May I ask a question? Is the hon. member not aware that he is preaching a very advanced doctrine of state socialism?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
No, I Ao not und-rstand anything about state socialism; I understand ordinary business common sense, that is all.
I have been a business man for many years and I want to see business go ahead in this country, and go ahead just as much in the prairie section as in the other parts of this Dominion. That is all I am trying to get at, and if I am wrong I will acknowledge it quite freely before this House.

The Address*-Mr. Marler
I was going on to say when these theories came up for discussion that we might well consider what the objections are in connection with this much debated subject of tariffs. To those who are opposed to a reasonable tariff for this country I will say that if any of the objections they urge are well founded I shall be the first to favour the wiping out of the objectionable features. What are these objections? The commonest one is that the tariff promotes inefficiency. I do not know whether it does or does not. The second objection is that the manufacturer is taking improper advantage of the tariff. I say again that I do not know whether he is or is not. Another objection is that insufficient revenue is procured from the country on account of the tariff framed as it is and on account of the manner in which it is collected. That may be the case. Another objection, and the last, is that it fosters industries in Canada w'hich enjoy no reasonable measure of success. Now all these objections are objections which, to my way of thinking, and I say it quite frankly, should be investigated. I say further: If any of these objections are well founded I will be the first to stand up in this House and say, "Wipe that objection away."

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Wipe the objection
away?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Nothing could be fairer
than that. I do not think I could be conscientiously asked to support a tariff that has these objectionable features in it; I do not intend to support a tariff that has any such features in it.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I should have
thought you would allow the objections.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Did my friend say "Wipe
them out?"

speechtext: Allow the objections.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I cannot hear my hon.
friend.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: My hon. friend said that if the abjection was good he would wipe it out. I do not think he meant to say that.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am afraid my hon. friend from West York is becoming a theorist also. Sooner or later he will have to seat himself beside my hon. friend the member from Brant (Mr. Good). When that takes place we shall be most delighted to have the joint theories of these two gentlemen. No, I am getting away from theories and trying to get down to
facts. In discussing this subject what I want lo know, and what hon. gentlemen want to know, is this: Does our present tariff prevent what it should prevent, and does it effect what it should effect? No one can say that it does, and no one can say that it does not. It was in 1907 and since then there have been hundreds and hundreds of changes in the tariff. Now I claim, and I think I correctly claim, that there should be a complete revision of that tariff based on present day conditions and in keeping with what the conditions may be. I go further and say this: That the only way by which that can be brought about is to (have a properly constituted tariff board to investigate every item and to find out whether any item is right or wrong. I say that to make our tariff on a hit or miss principle will get us nowhere. We may be imposing burdens we Should not impose; there may be disqualifications in the tariff which should not be there and which certainly should be wiped out. But how are we going to find out unless the matter is submitted to a proper tariff board? I do not mean a tariff board that shall make the tariff. That is nonsense; the government will have to take the responsibility itself of making the tariff. I do not intend this to be a board such as functions in the United States, with public hearings or anything of that kind; but we want a board of experts in this country to look into tariff matters continually, to say what is right and what is wrong, and to keep the government fully advised. The Prime Minister mentioned this very fully in his speech on May 15 last, and I am using very largely the very words of the leader of the government.
I have nearly finished every hon. member will be glad to hear, unless there are some more theories to be answered. During the past year, and notably during the past few weeks, we have heard all kinds of reports as regards Canada. We have beard reports as to our expenditures, reports as regards the exodus of our population, and many other reports of the worst kind. I think there is a great deal in certain of these reports and that they will bear careful investigation. My hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woods-worth) in his very able speech brought up some the other day. All these cases deserve consideration. There is no good burying our heads in the sand and saying everything is beautiful in this country. We have to investigate facts as we find them, and unless we do investigate we will never go ahead. We have heard from within that "Confederation is at stake," and from without that "Our
The Address-Mr. Marler

path is laid to the cave of a dragon with stars on its forehead and stripes on its side, only waiting a favourable opportunity to consume us." All these things we have heard about our country but t'he peculiar fact is that notwithstanding all these criticisms which have taken place, all these matters which have happened, very few remedies have been brought forward in order to effect a solution. The criticisms have been ample, but the solutions few and far between. I do not wonder at that particular situation. The people of this country are generally working at fever heat. They have no time to particularly investigate national affairs. They know these affairs in a general sort of way. Still, I doubt very much if they know that our national railways have cost $2,000,000,000; I doubt very much if they know that our canals 'have cost $130,000,000; I doubt very much if they know that we have invested in manufacturing industries in this country over $3,000,000,000. What they do ask is that this vast structure erected, and perhaps unwisely erected, should be made to pay and that taxation should be reduced. They ask us in the meantime to forget our party differences, to some extent at least, and to get down to a reasonable and proper basis and go ahead. After we go ahead and after taxation is reduced we may come down to our party tactics again. But in the meantime-

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Why go back to party?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Again I am not a hazy
theorist. I think these things are practical, but I say that in the meantime we should sink any differences we have and try and evolve some policy which will be good and beneficial to the whole of Canada. I say quite frankly, as I said earlier in these observations, that to make a blanket policy for this country is impossible. I say again, as I have said before that comoensating factors will have to be given in various sections of the country and the objection taken by my hon. friend the member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) was .perfectly correct in every way. These compensating factors- the helping of the Maritimes, the helping of the central provinces in a certain way, the helping of the prairie sections in a certain way-will, I know, cost money. I ask: What are we to do, where are we to land, where are we to get off, unless we promote profitable production, unless we get more people into the country. We spend money in immigration every year-the Minister of Immigration and 'Colonization carries out as good a policy as anyone can carry out-but no policy of immigration, no amount of

money spent in immigration, no advertising or propaganda of any kind, will have any lasting or enduring effect unless the people of this country at the present rime are prosperous and are engaged in profitable production, and this is the first thing that must be brought about.
Now, what are the alternatives? The alternatives are these:	For the people of
Canada to make a bold and courageous stand, cost monetarily what it will, for the purpose of building up our population and establishing profitable production. When the population arrives, when that production and further production takes place, any necessity of compensating factors will then cease, and the cost will seem trifling. But if we do not do that, if we do not take our courage in our hands and say that we will help here and we will help there and go ahead in the meantime, what will be the result? We will lose population. More than that we will not be able to keep this great structure we have erected with less people, and then we may find ourselves unknowingly but certainly treading the path towards that cave and that dragon which I spoke of a few moments ago. Why Sir, it is impossible for me to think that we Canadians lack courage in this country. It is impossible for me to think that we have forgotten what our forefathers have done in Canada. It is impossible for me, coming as I do from the province of Quebec, to forget what our French Canadians have done in old Quebec, how they built up that province out of the wilderness, and how the Anglo-Saxon race built up the province of Ontario, the prairie provinces and the province of British Columbia over the Rocky mountains. It is impossible for me to forget these things. It is impossible for me, even in the shortest space of time the human imagination is able to conceive, to believe that we have not in Canada the courage to take this situation in hand; and to bring forward, as I say cost what it will, reasonable and proper policies to encourage profitable production throughout this land, using that policy to provide production and more people. The only way we can get more people, I repeat, is by that production. Give us more people and we will hear nothing about Canada's troubles, we will hear nothing about freight rates or any of these other matters, and the country will blossom like the rose.
